title: SAP ADT MCP: Results from a 20-Tool Hands-on Evaluation
subtitle: Trial-system RAP generation, save-sequence ABAP Unit, ATC and documented tool limitations
evidence_status: Closed R2 trial assessment; evidence reviewed with explicit limitations; not production qualification
lineage_note: R7 restores the full research depth of the private R3 research master, corrected by the closed KS01 R2 findings. Sentences approved in R5 are retained verbatim; R3 observations are kept as explicitly historical evidence.

sections.title: Executive summary
sections.markdown:
**What SAP ADT MCP provides.** ABAP Development Tools for Visual Studio Code ships a built-in ADT MCP Server. SAP's tutorial (modified 2026-09-17) lists 13 tools for listing destinations, creating ABAP objects, generating RAP objects, activating, running ABAP Unit, running ATC and handling transports. In the live trial assessment reported here (KS01 R2) the connected server exposed **20 tools**. The two counts are different evidence scopes and are not merged into one inventory (see the MCP tool inventory tab).

**Why it matters.** It gives an AI coding agent a typed, auditable way to perform ADT operations that used to be reachable only through a user interface. The agent calls a generator tool instead of a person clicking through a wizard. That is a real change in how development operations can be orchestrated.

**What the agent contributes.** The model plans, chooses tools, drafts ABAP source and interprets results. The MCP server exposes operations and does not reason. MCP is a protocol: a server may expose code-generation or source-writing operations, and the ADT MCP Server inspected exposes RAP generation but no general-purpose arbitrary source-read or source-write operation.

**What the integration can and cannot do.** In the configuration tested, the server could create objects from metadata, run a RAP generator, activate objects by file URI, run ABAP Unit and ATC, and read transports and service bindings. It exposed no tool that reads or writes arbitrary ABAP source. Source editing happened through the VS Code editor over the `abap:` virtual filesystem, which is what SAP's own agent instructions describe.

**What the closed R2 experiment established.** A RAP generator run reported 14 related repository artifacts for a student-management business object. A developer agent implemented a save-time validation; three ABAP Unit tests that drive the RAP save sequence ran with an overall PASS; the final ATC worklist reported five open P2/P3 findings; and an OData V4 service was published and discovered. It did **not** establish OData runtime behaviour, update/delete coverage, authorization behaviour, or an independent read-back of the final source.

**Engineering conclusion.** Treat ADT MCP as an orchestration surface for ADT operations, not as an autonomous ABAP coding environment. Object creation succeeding is not evidence that a business requirement is implemented. SAP itself labels the server experimental and not for productive use.

sections.title: What was evaluated
sections.markdown: In a trial ABAP environment, the connected ADT MCP Server exposed 20 tools. A RAP student-management scenario generated 14 related repository artifacts. Activation tools, ATC runs, service discovery and ABAP Unit were exercised. SAP describes the ADT MCP Server as experimental and not intended for productive use.

sections.title: Evaluation method: six stages
sections.markdown:
The research followed one six-stage method. Each section in this note names the stage it belongs to, so a statement can be traced to the question it answers.

| Stage | Question | What was done in KS01 | Where to read it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DISCOVER | What does SAP actually offer, and what does the live server actually expose? | Read SAP's tutorials; captured the live tool schemas and destinations | SAP official offering; MCP tool inventory |
| EVALUATE | What would each tool do, and what could it change? | Classified tools by read, write and server-side execution; checked prerequisites and mutating behaviour before calling anything | MCP tool inventory; Architecture |
| ALIGN WITH HANDS-ON | Which realistic development scenario exercises those tools? | Chose a bounded RAP student-management scenario with owner-approved write boundaries | Hands-on evidence |
| PROVE | What do the receipts and test results actually show? | Executed generation, activation, ABAP Unit and ATC; recorded each outcome and its evidence class | Hands-on evidence; MCP tool inventory |
| COMPARE | How does this compare with the alternatives and with the documented intent? | Compared documented tools with observed tools, and MCP-assisted work with manual and template-based approaches | Comparative assessment |
| IMPROVE | What should change, and what remains open? | Recorded defects, limitations, recommendations and the next experiments | Conclusions and recommendations |

The site-wide lifecycle strip uses the labels IDENTIFY and SCOPE FOR IMPROVEMENT for the first and last stages; they mean the same as DISCOVER and IMPROVE here.

sections.title: Problem statement: four modes that are routinely conflated
sections.markdown:
Four things are routinely conflated:

| Mode | Who writes the logic | Who performs system operations | Where the proof comes from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Traditional ABAP development | Developer | Developer in ADT (Eclipse or VS Code) | Developer-run activation, ABAP Unit, ATC, review |
| AI-assisted ABAP development | Model drafts, developer pastes or edits | Developer | Same as above; the model adds speed, not proof |
| MCP-enabled tool orchestration | Model drafts; an editor-integrated agent can write into the editor | Agent calls MCP tools (create, activate, test, ATC) | Tool responses from SAP, still needing independent interpretation |
| Fully automated development | Model | Agent | Would need requirement-to-test traceability; not demonstrated here |

**Why object creation is not proof.** A generator creating a CDS view, behavior definition and service binding shows that a template was instantiated. It says nothing about whether a rating must be between 1 and 5, whether duplicate reviews are rejected, or whether a calculation is correct. Those rules live in source that a template does not contain. The only proof that a requirement is met is an executed test of that requirement, ideally against a read-back of the activated object.

sections.title: How to read the evidence
sections.markdown:
Every material statement in this note belongs to a claim in the evidence register (References and supporting evidence tab). Each claim carries an evidence class and a scope.

**Evidence classes.**

| Class | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| SAP_DOCUMENTED | Stated on an SAP page or repository read for this research |
| TOOL_CONTRACT_VERIFIED | Read from a live tool listing or a tool schema |
| SAP_LIVE_VERIFIED | A response from the live trial system through the MCP server |
| LOCAL_EXECUTION_VERIFIED | Observed in our own local execution |
| MCP_REPORTED and related classes | Reported by an MCP tool response in the final KS01 R2 assessment; the curated receipts are summaries, not raw transcripts |
| AGENT_SOURCE_PLUS_MCP_RESPONSE, EDITOR_AGENT_REPORTED | Source or a diagnosis supplied by the SAP developer agent in VS Code, combined with MCP results |
| OWNER_REPORTED | Stated by the research owner; not independently verified |
| OBSERVED_LIMITATION, NOT_VERIFIED | A limit that was observed, or something that was not established |

**Scopes.** *R2 current* is the closed KS01 R2 assessment and is the factual baseline. *R3 historical* is an earlier baseline hands-on that used a different scenario, a different object set and a different trial session. Its observations are kept because they explain how the investigation evolved, but they are never mixed into R2 results. *SAP documented* is what SAP's pages state. *Superseded* marks an earlier statement that a later result replaced.

Hash-verifying the evidence archive establishes that the packaged bytes are intact. It does not establish direct access to the SAP system.

sections.markdown:

Dates were taken from the pages' own metadata and visible "Created on" lines: the ADT MCP tutorial was created 2026-09-01 and modified 2026-09-17; the other two tutorials were modified 2026-10-06 and 2026-09-30; the RAP130 repository was last pushed 2026-06-03. Tutorials change; re-check before relying on a specific tool name or restriction.

| ADT MCP Server | Enabled in the extension; 13 tools listed by name; "experimental feature that may change at any time without notice. It is not intended for productive use." | C01, C02 |

| RAP130 workshop | Builds a transactional Fiori elements app with RAP in VS Code using the ADT MCP Server and a coding agent; requires "SAP Joule for developers, ABAP AI capabilities" enabled; Copilot is the primary tested agent; Apache-2.0 | C06 |
| ABAP Cloud, RAP, ABAP Unit, ATC | Part of the ABAP Cloud development model in the cited tutorials; ABAP Unit and ATC are exposed as MCP tools | C02, C05 |

sections.title: How to interpret the official offering
sections.markdown:
- The server is **experimental** by SAP's own statement. Nothing in this note presents it as production-ready.
- The tutorial's tool list and the tool lists observed on live systems differ in count and in some names (see the MCP tool inventory tab).
- Joule for developers is a prerequisite of the RAP130 workshop. It was not part of our hands-on, so no Joule claim is made from our evidence.
- SAP's tutorials describe intended behaviour. They are not execution evidence, and none of our results is a statement about SAP's other systems or releases.

sections.title: Reference architecture: two paths into the system
sections.markdown:
The diagram shows two paths into the ABAP system. The **tool-invocation path** is MCP protocol calls to typed operations. The **source-editing path** is editor integration through VS Code and the `abap:` virtual filesystem. Both end in the ABAP repository, where activation, ABAP Unit and ATC run server side and return the execution evidence.

**Accessible text explanation.**

1. A **business requirement** reaches the **AI model**. The model, wrapped by an **agent orchestration** loop, decides what to do next.
2. For system operations, the agent uses an **MCP client** to call the **SAP ADT MCP Server**. These calls are typed operations: list destinations, create an object from metadata, run a RAP generator, activate objects by URI, run ABAP Unit, run ATC, read transports and service bindings. This is the tool-invocation path.
3. For **source code**, the path is different. The agent must write into the file the ADT extension exposes through VS Code's `abap:` virtual filesystem, using editor APIs. This is the source-editing path. It does not go through any tool observed on the MCP server.
4. The two paths meet in the **ABAP repository**. Activation, ABAP Unit and ATC then run server side and return results; those results, not the agent's narrative, are the execution evidence.
5. A **human** approves boundaries (system, package, names, transport) and reviews outcomes.

sections.title: Where ADT MCP fits
sections.markdown: ADT MCP is a typed tool interface within a broader agent-assisted workflow. Its value is in exposing controlled SAP operations. It does not replace the coding agent, IDE, SAP authorizations, executable tests or governance.

sections.title: Protocol capability versus server capability
sections.markdown:
MCP is a protocol: it defines how a client discovers and calls tools that a server chooses to expose. A server may expose generation tools, source-writing tools, both or neither; the protocol itself guarantees none of them. What a specific server offers is determined by its tool list.

The ADT MCP Server inspected exposes RAP generation but no general-purpose source read or write tool. So "uses MCP" and "can write ABAP source" are independent properties; for ADT, the second depends on the agent host and the editor integration. The responsibilities differ: the **model** drafts, the **generator implementation** (server side) instantiates templates, and the **editor integration** writes into the file the system exposes.

sections.title: Why this server is not a complete autonomous coding environment
sections.markdown:
- No tool reads or writes ABAP source.
- The create-object tool accepts metadata only; its description says the content must not contain source.
- The activation and unit-test tools take URIs of files in the VS Code virtual filesystem and expect them to be saved first; they presuppose an editor that has already written the source.
- There is no delete tool and no direct activation-state read tool in the inspected lists.

Each of these is a finding about the tested tool lists. It is not a statement about other builds, other agents' own tools, or future releases.

sections.title: Source-editing path
sections.markdown: Custom ABAP source was handled through a compatible VS Code SAP developer-agent editing path, rather than a general-purpose MCP source-write tool. The editor-agent-provided source and MCP test results support the reported lifecycle; an independent live source readback was not available to the reviewer.

sections.title: Security and governance
sections.markdown:
- **SAP system authorization.** Every MCP call executes with the SAP user's authorizations. The agent has no authority beyond the logged-in user.
- **ADT session authority.** The MCP server relies on the VS Code extension's authenticated destination; expiry shows as a "user was logged off" response. Do not extract or reuse session credentials to work around this.
- **MCP tool permissions.** The server advertises no read-only or destructive hints, so a client or reviewer cannot rely on annotations. Maintain your own allowlist.
- **Agent authority.** A model that can call the generator can create many objects at once. Treat that as a write with blast radius. In KS01 R2 the agent host's permission classifier denied the object-creation and AI-fix tool calls; the boundary was respected, not bypassed.
- **Human approval boundaries.** Approve system, package, names and transport before generation. An earlier baseline run produced doubled-prefix object names after the names had been approved, because the approved names were not what the tool produced; verify the planned object list against the tool's naming rules before calling.
- **Repository source protection.** The `abap:` filesystem is the system of record; local copies are not authoritative.
- **Transport governance.** The transport query used in the evidence is not discriminating (see the tool inventory): it returned the same answer for a package that does not exist. Productive use requires transport and change control that this evidence does not cover.
- **Activation versus functional validation.** An activated object and a clean ATC run are not proof of correct behavior.

sections.markdown:
Several bodies of evidence exist. They come from different sources, sessions and times, and are **not merged into one live inventory**.

| Scope | What it is | Date / build | Tools | Reliability for "what this server does" |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| S: SAP tutorial | The tool table on SAP's "Enable the ADT MCP Server" page | Page created 2026-09-01, modified 2026-09-17 | 13 entries | Documents intended tools; says nothing about a given system or build |
| R: Earlier discovery | An authenticated discovery of "ADT MCP Server 1.0.0" recorded in the workbench's earlier tool review | Date and extension build not stated in the record | 20 tools | A real listing from one session; no version evidence |
| E: Baseline hands-on session | The tool list seen in the earlier baseline hands-on (2026-10-13), plus the calls actually executed against SAP | 2026-10-13; extension 1.1.2 installed locally | 20 tools listed; 9 tool families executed | Strongest for "what ran" in that session; server build not recorded |
| D: Partial schemas | Input fields recorded in the baseline receipts (create_object, activate_objects, run_unit_tests, generator schema, transport-get, fetch_services) | 2026-10-13 | subset | Fields only; complete input and output schemas were not captured |

sections.title: Why some tools did not PASS
sections.markdown:
The object-creation and AI-fix tools were rejected by the agent host's permission classifier. The permission boundary was respected, not bypassed. The transport-difference tool lacked a valid transport to inspect and the AI-fix-result tool lacked a real AI-fix job. The transport-creation tool was deliberately skipped by owner instruction.

These outcomes are disclosed as what they are. They are not tool failures, and they are not successful positive paths. The tally contains no whole-tool FAIL, but it is not 20 tools demonstrated on a successful positive path.

sections.title: Absent categories and what R2 added
sections.markdown:
**Absent categories** (absent from the 20-tool lists in scopes R, E and L): read ABAP source, write ABAP source, delete an object, list package contents, read activation status, publish a service binding. Absence is established for those lists only; it is not a statement about other builds, other agents' own tools, or future releases.

**Tutorial tool classes and what KS01 R2 added.** The earlier baseline had not exercised activation, ABAP Unit, AI fix, quick fixes or transport creation. KS01 R2 exercised activation and ABAP Unit with real passing and failing runs, ran deterministic quick fixes (a no-op, a null-pointer error on an empty worklist, and no applied fix), had AI fix blocked by the permission classifier, and skipped transport creation by owner decision.

sections.title: KS01 R2: generated RAP artifact inventory
sections.markdown:
The generator response reported 14 related repository artifacts with generator-determined names: a database table; CDS root and projection views; behavior definitions for the root and the projection; metadata extension and access-control artifacts; two behavior pool classes; a service definition and a service binding; and paired companion artifacts of the NONT and RONT kinds.

Do not infer an independently enumerated activation status for all 14 artifacts from the generator response alone. The final ATC inventory covered 13 of them and did not check the RONT companion.

sections.title: RAP validation and ABAP Unit
sections.markdown:
The final test implementation contained three methods for a valid status, missing name and invalid status. They exercised the RAP business-object save sequence using `MODIFY ENTITIES` and `COMMIT ENTITIES` with an OSQL test double; the MCP runner reported an overall PASS. The test result omitted a per-method count, so the three cases are established from the final editor-agent source excerpt.

Earlier failures were traced to RAP transactional-buffer leakage across tests. A `ROLLBACK ENTITIES` call in test setup provided isolation. This diagnosis is supported by the packaged test history, not by a fresh direct SAP repository readback from the reviewer.

sections.title: KS01 R2: the business validation in detail
sections.markdown:
The behavior definition declares a validation that runs on save for create and update, over two fields: the name and the status. The implemented handler rejects an empty name and permits only the status values ACTIVE, INACTIVE and GRADUATED.

The three final test methods cover a valid record, an empty name and an invalid status. Each uses RAP EML `MODIFY ENTITIES` and `COMMIT ENTITIES` rather than merely calling a helper method, and an OSQL test double isolates persistence for the table. The two negative cases assert the reported validation message and the rejection; the positive case asserts that nothing was rejected or reported and that the row reached the double.

**Supported conclusion:** RAP business-object save-sequence validation exercised by ABAP Unit with an OSQL test double, overall PASS.

**Not supported:** end-to-end OData HTTP validation, update and delete coverage, authorization verification, or acceptance as a production-grade business application.

sections.title: KS01 R2: why earlier test runs failed, and the diagnosis that was withdrawn
sections.markdown:
Earlier test runs failed repeatedly. Failed records left in the RAP transactional buffer by the negative tests were re-validated in later test methods, so the valid-record test saw exactly two failed lines that belonged to the previous cases. The ninth test iteration added `ROLLBACK ENTITIES` in the test class setup, and the tenth removed a temporary diagnostic method that was failing on purpose. The handler and the behavior definition were unchanged after the fifth iteration.

An earlier diagnosis, that the validation's entity read returned initial values, was **wrong** and was withdrawn: the empty-name test passed with the status read correctly. The agent's conclusion was treated as a claim, and an independent re-run plus cross-test reasoning identified the buffer leakage. The evidence supports the test-isolation diagnosis; it is not a new root-cause experiment.

sections.title: KS01 R2: activation and what the evidence supports
sections.markdown:
Activation through the MCP activation tool returned success for the development objects, and subsequent ATC runs resolved the activated objects. The evidence does not contain an independent read-back of the active state of every one of the 14 generated artifacts, and no MCP tool in the inspected lists returns activation status. The supportable statement is therefore "activation operations returned success", not "all 14 artifacts were independently verified active".

Publishing the service binding is not an MCP tool; the owner performed it in the ADT editor. The business-service tools then reported the binding as published, with the entity set discovered. That is service metadata discovery; it is separate from runtime acceptance of the service.

sections.title: OData service
sections.markdown: The OData V4 service was reported published and its entity metadata retrieved. No HTTP runtime functional request was executed, so OData-level business behavior was not established.

sections.title: ATC result
sections.markdown: The final ATC worklist reported five open priority-2/priority-3 findings, mainly message-literal and test-code SELECT hygiene issues. These were not waived or presented as an ATC-clean result.

sections.title: KS01 R2: final ATC findings in detail
sections.markdown:
Final worklist contents, as reported:

| Priority | Finding | Location | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P3 | SLIN 1700 (two findings) | Behavior pool class | Message literals without text elements |
| P3 | AMB_SINGLE | Test include | Single-row selection hygiene |
| P2 | No WHERE condition (two findings) | Test include | Test SELECT statements without a WHERE clause |

An earlier SLIN 1205 finding was cleared. An earlier worklist had reported the behavior definitions and the projection behavior class clean. The final report is curated text, not a raw SAP JSON transcript; the RONT companion was not covered. This is an ATC-executed result with five findings, not an ATC-clean application, and it is not evidence that functional defects cannot exist.

sections.title: Deterministic quickfix
sections.markdown: The deterministic quickfix tool produced a null-pointer error when invoked on an empty ATC worklist. On a nonempty worklist without an applicable fix, it returned an empty, non-error result. No actual deterministic quickfix application was demonstrated. Permission blocks were respected rather than overridden.

sections.title: Illustrative business requirement and who can do each step
sections.markdown:
**Requirement (illustrative).** A book review has ISBN, title, author, rating, text and reviewer. The rating must be an integer from 1 to 5; a violating save must be rejected with a message. This scenario is illustrative and was not an executed KS01 scenario.

**Development journey and who can do each step.**

| Stage | What happens | Tested MCP in the earlier baseline | What happened in KS01 R2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirement | Written by a human | Not applicable | Student-management validation defined by the owner |
| Data model | Table and CDS views from the generator | Yes: generator tool | Yes: 14 artifacts |
| ABAP business logic | Validation in the behavior implementation class | No tool; needs editor or agent integration | Written by the SAP developer agent in the VS Code editor |
| Object creation | Generated, or the create-object tool | Yes | Generated; the create-object tool was permission blocked |
| Source modification | Write into the behavior implementation | Not through MCP; the owner edited manually | Through the SAP developer agent, not through MCP |
| Activation | Activation tool by file URI | Yes, once source is saved in the editor | Yes: several successful responses |
| Testing | Unit-test tool | Tool exists; not executed | Executed: failing and passing runs, final overall PASS |
| Evidence | ATC worklists, service binding state | Worklists and binding state read; behaviour not | Worklists, binding state and unit result read; OData runtime not |

**Illustrative logic (NOT SAP-activated, NOT compiled, NOT tested, NOT part of KS01 R2):**

```abap
" ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY - not created, activated or run in any SAP system.
METHOD validateRating.
  READ ENTITIES OF zr_review IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Review FIELDS ( Rating ) WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys )
    RESULT DATA(reviews).
  LOOP AT reviews INTO DATA(review) WHERE Rating < 1 OR Rating > 5.
    APPEND VALUE #( %tky = review-%tky ) TO failed-review.
    APPEND VALUE #( %tky = review-%tky
                    %msg = new_message_with_text( severity = if_abap_behv_message=>severity-error
                                                  text     = 'Rating must be between 1 and 5' ) )
      TO reported-review.
  ENDLOOP.
ENDMETHOD.
```

Names such as `validateRating` assume a validation declared in the behavior definition; nothing here was checked against generated objects.

sections.title: Source-write investigation (historical) and the R2 outcome
sections.markdown:
Three options were evaluated for getting agent-written source into SAP in the earlier baseline:

- **A (a tool in the MCP server):** rejected, no such tool exists.
- **B (editor integration reachable from Claude Code):** not reachable from the tools available in the tested session. The `abap:` path was not visible to local file tools, and no editor-API tool was exposed to the model. This is "not established in this configuration", not "impossible".
- **C (direct ADT REST adapter reusing a session):** not selected; it would require session or credential reuse and unverified endpoints.

The research workbench's own ADT adapter is deliberately read-only, with a short allowlist of read tools, one allowed destination and write verbs refused. The investigation was closed as an accepted limitation.

**What KS01 R2 added.** Option B was realized through a different route: the owner launched SAP's own `abap-developer` agent in VS Code, and that agent read and edited source over the `abap:` virtual filesystem. Claude Code itself still could not read or write that filesystem; it verified through MCP activation, ABAP Unit and ATC. This is a host-integration boundary, not a general conclusion that agents cannot edit ABAP.

sections.title: Evidence boundary
sections.markdown:
The distinction that matters is *SAP system execution* (responses from the live trial system through the MCP server) versus *local or tool-schema discovery* (inspecting tool lists and extension files). Tool-schema discovery shows what is offered, not what works.

A further boundary applies to source. The final ABAP source was supplied by the SAP developer agent; it was not independently read back from the live repository by Claude Code or by the independent reviewer, and most MCP receipts in the archive are curated summaries, not unedited wire-level transcripts.

sections.title: Failures, accepted limitations and incorrect assumptions
sections.markdown:
**What worked in KS01 R2:** tool listing and classification, generation of 14 artifacts, activation, ABAP Unit with real failing and passing runs, ATC worklists with priorities, and service discovery after publishing.

**What failed or was blocked in KS01 R2:** earlier unit-test iterations failed from transactional-buffer leakage; the object-creation and AI-fix tools were permission blocked; the deterministic quickfix tool raised a null-pointer error on an empty worklist; two tools lacked a prerequisite for a positive path.

**What failed in the earlier baseline:** a logged-off session on one destination; generator run 1 validation rejection; a generator schema call timeout (retry succeeded); two validation payload errors; preview automation without an SAP session; the `abap:` filesystem not readable by local tools.

**What was not tested:** OData HTTP functional and negative-path requests, update and delete paths, authorization scenarios, transport creation, a deterministic quickfix that actually applies a fix, an AI fix, a Copilot or other compatible-agent run, and Joule for developers.

**Assumptions that proved incorrect:**

- That the generator's `prefix` is a bare prefix; it is applied in addition to the generator's own naming, producing doubled-prefix objects.
- That an ADT MCP server would offer source write; none is present.
- That the tutorial tool names equal the server's names; they differ.
- That SAP's tutorial pages carry no date; the page metadata shows creation and modification dates.
- That a validation read returned initial values; the failures were buffer leakage between tests.

**Accepted limitations:** no arbitrary source write via the tested MCP path; no object delete tool; no activation read-back; cleanup of the baseline run's objects is an owner action in ADT.

**Optional versus essential:** a source-write adapter is optional for knowledge sharing and was closed. A compatible-agent hands-on with Copilot in VS Code would be the natural next experiment, but it is not required to state the findings above.

sections.title: Scope: the MCP interface versus the surrounding workflow
sections.markdown: This is a focused assessment of SAP ABAP Development Tools MCP, not a new attempt to establish whether agent-assisted SAP development can work end to end. Broader engineering workflows may combine models, coding agents, VS Code, SAP development tools and human approval. We evaluated what the MCP interface contributes, what was executed and what remains dependent on other components.

sections.title: RAP generator versus custom business logic
sections.markdown:
**A. Predefined generator functionality.** The generator tool instantiated a template from a schema and a field list. In the KS01 R2 hands-on it produced 14 related repository artifacts: a database table, CDS root and projection views, metadata and access-control artifacts, behavior definitions, behavior pool classes, a service definition and binding, and paired companion artifacts. This is genuine, useful scaffolding. The repository was not independently enumerated.

**B. Arbitrary business requirements.** A rule such as "status must be one of three values" is a validation in the behavior implementation, or a CDS constraint, or a determination. A generator template has no input for that rule. The generator can create the class shell; the logic is source that someone must write.

**C. Agent-generated source.** A model can propose that source. In KS01 R2 the SAP developer agent drafted and wrote the validation handler and the test include in the editor, and the MCP unit-test and ATC tools then ran against it. In the earlier baseline, by contrast, an AI-drafted test class existed only as a local file marked not created, not compiled and not run; its existence was the only fact established.

**D. IDE-based implementation.** SAP's own agent definition says to add and edit source via the VS Code editor, opening the editor first using the provided file paths, then activating. Completing step C therefore depends on a compatible agent host that can write into the editor. Whether a given agent can do this against the `abap:` filesystem is a property of that agent, not of MCP. Claude Code in the tested sessions could not; SAP's own `abap-developer` agent could.

**Takeaway.** A generator can create functional RAP artifacts without any general-purpose source-editing API. The gap between "scaffold" and "implemented requirement" is exactly the source-editing step, and the proof that it was closed is the executed test.

sections.title: Comparative engineering assessment
sections.markdown:
Qualitative only. No performance, cost, maturity or productivity percentages or scores are claimed, because none were measured. Every cell depends on the SAP release, environment, tool support, agent access, authentication and authorization in use; none is a guarantee of compatibility or capability on another system.

| Dimension | Eclipse ADT manual | VS Code ADT manual | ADT MCP plus Claude Code (tested) | Compatible VS Code agent workflow | Template-based RAP generation | Custom ABAP source implementation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capability coverage | Eclipse ADT feature set for the connected system type; not assessed here | Core ADT per SAP tutorial | Creation, generation, activation, ABAP Unit, ATC, transport reads, service discovery; no source tool in the inspected set | Tools plus editor edit; the SAP developer agent was exercised in R2, Copilot was not | Scaffolding for patterns the generator supports | Depends on release, authorization and the developer |
| Source writing | Yes | Yes | **No** from Claude Code (not reachable); source was written by the SAP developer agent | Yes via the SAP developer agent in R2; other agents not verified | None beyond the template | Required |
| Authentication | Interactive SAP login | Interactive SAP login | Reused destination session; logoff errors seen in the baseline | Same destination model | Same | Same |
| Authorization | SAP user authorizations | Same | Same user authorizations, plus the agent host's tool permissions | Same, plus agent permission | Same | Same |
| Developer control | Direct | Direct | Tool-call approvals; one generator call creates many objects; classifier blocked two writes in R2 | Depends on the agent | Parameter-level | Direct |
| Testability | ABAP Unit and ATC available in the tool | ABAP Unit and ATC per SAP tutorial | ATC and ABAP Unit executed through MCP in R2 | Unit tool plus editor-written tests; exercised in R2 | Needs custom tests for custom logic | Depends on test design and execution |
| Reproducibility | Manual | Manual | Receipts exist; the prefix defect shows input sensitivity | Depends on the agent | Deterministic for the same input | Depends on process |
| Operational readiness | Not assessed in this work | Not assessed in this work | MCP server experimental per SAP | MCP server experimental per SAP | Generator readiness not assessed beyond trial runs; MCP wrapper experimental | Not assessed in this work |

| Principal limitation | Manual effort | Manual effort | No source path from this client; final source agent-reported | Agent and editor dependency | Cannot express custom rules | Effort |

sections.title: CAPELLA and Synapse: context, not KS01 evidence
sections.markdown:
Earlier CAPELLA and Synapse engineering explored broader AI-assisted SAP development workflows involving VS Code, Claude Code, implementation, activation, testing and integration. They provide separate architectural context. They are not execution receipts for the KS01 tool inventory, and no KS01 result is attributed to them.

KS01 R2 is therefore not a fresh claim that AI agents can develop ABAP applications end to end. It is a focused, evidence-based assessment of SAP ADT MCP's 20 exposed tools and their role inside that larger engineering architecture. No controlled productivity, cost or latency figures were measured.

sections.title: Conclusion and limits
sections.markdown: The exercise demonstrates a useful development-tool workflow and candid limitations; it is not a production-readiness assessment, a productivity benchmark, or an all-tools-PASS claim.

sections.title: Engineering recommendations
sections.markdown:
| Category | Recommendation |
| --- | --- |
| Usable now (per our evidence, on a trial system) | Use generators for scaffolding; activate and run ABAP Unit and ATC through the tools once source is saved; read service binding state; list destinations and generator schemas |
| Supported with prerequisites | ADT for VS Code, a supported ABAP system, an authenticated destination; Joule for developers for the SAP workshop scenario |
| Requires compatible tooling | Source editing and activation by URI need an agent that supports VS Code's virtual workspace filesystem; the SAP developer agent was exercised, other agents were not |
| Experimental or restricted | The whole ADT MCP Server per SAP; do not use it on productive systems |
| Not independently verified | OData runtime behaviour, update and delete paths, authorization, transport creation, a deterministic quickfix that applies a fix, AI fix tools, a Copilot workflow, Joule |

sections.title: Practical rules
sections.markdown:
1. Validate the full list of objects a generator will create before calling it.
2. Never rely on a creation response as evidence of behavior.
3. Require an executed test per requirement, and run it against the activated code.
4. Record tool responses as receipts, and state which receipts are curated summaries.
5. Keep an explicit read-only allowlist, and respect the agent host's permission boundary rather than working around it.

sections.title: Lessons learned
sections.markdown:
1. A protocol capability is not a product capability. Evaluate the exact tools a server exposes.
2. Scaffolding and implementation are different milestones; only tests of the requirement prove the second.
3. The weakest link in an agent workflow is often the editor integration, not the model.
4. Absence of a tool is a finding. Record it.
5. Input conventions (like a generator `prefix`) are failure points; dry-run validation before write.
6. Without a read-back tool, "activated" can only be inferred.
7. Test isolation matters in RAP: a missing transactional-buffer reset made a correct handler look broken, and an agent's confident diagnosis was wrong until it was re-run independently.
8. A PASS summary can hide detail. The unit-test result carried no per-method count, and a tool tally of "no FAIL" must still carry the quickfix null-pointer defect.

sections.title: What an SAP architect should check
sections.markdown: Which tools are exposed and with what annotations; how source reaches the system and who can write it; whether tests are executed against activated code; whether a delete or rollback path exists; how authorization and transport are enforced; whether the agent host's permission model blocks writes you did not intend; the vendor's support statement.

sections.title: Next research opportunities
sections.markdown:
These are optional and are not prerequisites for publishing the closed R2 research honestly.

- **OData negative-path test.** Execute create, invalid-input and authorization requests against the published service, with approved cleanup.
- **A real quickfix application.** Exercise `abap_atc_execute_deterministic_quickfixes` when a genuine eligible finding exists. Adding text elements for the two message literals would also create such a candidate.
- **Update and delete coverage and authorization tests** for the validation.
- **Permission decisions** for the create-object and AI-fix tools, so their positive paths can be tested.
- **A compatible-agent hands-on** with GitHub Copilot in VS Code, to compare against the SAP developer agent.
- **Tooling feedback to SAP:** negative-path robustness of the quickfix tool, granular approval boundaries, and more complete read-back of activation state.

sections.title: Claims this research does not support
sections.markdown:
- "20 out of 20 tools passed" or "zero tool bugs".
- "The RAP service is fully functional over OData HTTP".
- "ATC clean" or "production ready".
- "All source was independently read from live SAP".
- "Measured productivity savings" or "cost or latency improvement".
- "Fully qualified" or "officially sealed" release status for this website.

sections.title: Frequently asked questions
sections.markdown:
**1. What does MCP actually do here?** MCP is a protocol that lets an agent discover and call a server's operations as typed tools. The ADT MCP Server exposes ADT operations such as listing, creating, generating, activating, testing and ATC. It does not reason; the model does. Whether a given MCP server can generate or write source depends on the tools it exposes.

**2. Does the ADT MCP Server generate ABAP source?** Its RAP generator tool instantiates objects from a template. We saw no tool that turns a requirement into custom business logic or writes arbitrary source into an object. Drafting custom source is done by the model; writing it needs an editor integration.

**3. Can it write ABAP source?** Not through any tool we inspected. SAP's agent instructions say source is edited in the VS Code editor. In KS01 R2 the SAP developer agent edited the source there; Claude Code itself could not.

**4. What can the RAP generators do?** Produce a consistent set of RAP artifacts for supported patterns (a UI service, a Web API service, a UI service from scratch on our system). They cannot express custom validations or calculations.

**5. Which agents work?** SAP states any agent that supports VS Code's virtual workspace filesystem; Copilot is confirmed. Claude Code in our tested sessions could not reach that filesystem; that is a statement about our configuration. SAP's own developer agent worked.

**6. Can I run ABAP Unit and ATC?** Yes, through the tools. In KS01 R2 we executed ABAP Unit with real failing and passing runs and a final overall PASS, and ATC with five open P2/P3 findings. ATC is a static check, and the unit result carries no per-method count.

**7. Did all 20 tools pass?** No. Thirteen passed, two passed with limitations, two were permission blocked, two lacked prerequisites for a positive test, and one was deliberately not tested. There is no whole-tool FAIL classification, but an empty-worklist quickfix null-pointer error was observed.

**8. Did the final ABAP Unit tests exercise RAP business validation?** The final source contains three tests using `MODIFY ENTITIES` and `COMMIT ENTITIES` with an OSQL test double, and the runner returned overall PASS. That establishes business-object save-sequence testing within that setup, not an OData HTTP end-to-end test.

**9. Why did earlier unit-test attempts fail?** The evidence supports cross-test contamination in the RAP transactional buffer. `ROLLBACK ENTITIES` in test setup addressed it. The source was supplied by the SAP developer agent and was not independently reread from the live repository.

**10. Was the service itself tested through OData?** No. Publication and metadata were observed, but no OData HTTP functional create, negative-path or authorization test was executed.

**11. Was ATC clean?** No. The final report retained five P2/P3 findings: message literals and test-code SELECT hygiene. They must not be described as resolved or as proof of production readiness.

**12. Is it secure?** It uses the logged-in user's SAP authorization, so it inherits that user's reach, and the server gives no tool annotations. Apply least privilege and your own allowlist; the agent host's permission model was an effective additional boundary in KS01 R2.

**13. Is it ready for production?** SAP says it is experimental and not intended for productive use. This was a bounded trial-system research exercise; no production qualification, speed comparison, latency benchmark or cost saving was established.

**14. What did CAPELLA and Synapse contribute?** Broader architectural context from separate engineering workflows. Their results were not counted as fresh KS01 R2 SAP execution receipts.

**15. What stays the developer's responsibility?** Requirements, source review, tests, transports, activation decisions, cleanup (there is no delete tool) and acceptance.

sections.title: Evidence provenance, review and authorship
sections.markdown:
**Evidence sources, in order of authority.** SAP's published documentation; the live tool contract (the tool listings and schemas); observed MCP responses from the trial system; reports from the SAP developer agent in VS Code (source and read-back); and independent inspection of the packaged evidence.

**Independent review.** A separate independent review of the closed R2 evidence archive returned ACCEPT_WITH_EXPLICIT_LIMITATIONS: the archive's integrity was verified, the tool matrix accepted with the quickfix defect disclosed, and publication permitted only with the limitations stated in this note. It is a research-publication acceptance, not an SAP productive-use approval. The evidence archive is kept privately; its SHA-256 is `b4934123a24865862f2b2b3e5cab0efa3cc037ad1f82346934b74cfaa803d30a`.

**Limits of that review.** It verified packaged bytes, not a connection to the SAP system. Several receipts are curated textual reconstructions. The final source is agent-reported, and no SAP system ID is established.

**Authorship and disclosure.** Independent technical research by Prasad Deshpande. The assessment was designed and directed by the owner. GPT supported editorial drafting and independent review of the supplied evidence package. Claude Code coordinated eligible SAP ADT MCP operations and verification, while a SAP developer agent in VS Code handled the ABAP source-editing path. The published findings distinguish tool responses, agent-reported source, documented SAP capabilities and untested areas. SAP, its products and trademarks belong to their respective owners; this independent publication is not affiliated with, approved by or endorsed by SAP.

**What was withheld from this public edition.** Private system and destination identifiers, package and object names, raw receipts and worklist identifiers, local file paths and the research workbench's internal controls.

claims.claim: Baseline ATC: 0 findings on 10 objects, and on 3 objects in a re-run.
claims.limitation: A different object set from KS01 R2; zero findings is not functional correctness

claims.claim: Baseline binding read-back: OData V4, published.
claims.limitation: Publisher of the binding not recorded

claims.claim: Baseline Fiori Elements launch and create, read, edit were reported working.
claims.limitation: Not independently verified

claims.claim: In the baseline, ABAP Unit and CRUD regression were not executed.
claims.limitation: Superseded for the KS01 R2 application, where ABAP Unit was executed

claims.claim: In the baseline, source editing was performed manually by the owner.
claims.limitation: No receipt of the edited source

claims.claim: In the baseline, an AI-drafted ABAP test class existed only as a local file marked not created, not compiled, not run.
claims.limitation: Existence only

claims.claim: Activation status was not read back from SAP; no tool in the inspected lists returns it.
claims.limitation: Still true in R2; ATC on active versions is indirect

claims.claim: The Claude Code VS Code extension exposes no generic write tool (static analysis; not runtime-tested).
claims.limitation: Static string scan

claims.claim: The tutorial spells createable and misspells the create-object row; receipts spell creatable.
claims.limitation: Spelling differences; version drift unverified

claims.claim: The tutorial lists 13 entries; the observed sessions list 20; 7 observed tools are absent from the tutorial table.
claims.limitation: Cause unverified: no version evidence for either list

claims.claim: The baseline transport query for the reference package returned no recording requirement and no requests; the target package classification was never read.
claims.limitation: Target package type not verified
